Program Definition pushout_apex_setoid {A B C : SetoidObject} (f : SetoidMorphism A B) (g : SetoidMorphism A C) : SetoidObject := {| carrier := Datatypes.sum (carrier B) (carrier C); is_setoid := {| equiv := pushout_eq f g; setoid_equiv := _ |} |}   — with `pushout_eq` the inductive closure generated by po_inl_cong, po_inr_cong, po_glue (`pushout_eq (inl (f a)) (inr (g a))`), po_sym, po_trans.

#[export] Program Instance FinSet_HasPushouts : HasPushouts FinSet := { pushout := fun x y z f g => {| Pull := po_apex f g; pullback_fst := po_in1 f g; pullback_snd := po_in2 f g |} }   — where `Definition po_apex : nat := fin_countP po_isrep` (Instance/FinSet/Pushout.v:406) is literally the number of connected components of the graph on y+z whose edges are `(inl (f i), inr (g i))`.

Program Definition Pullback_to_Universal {C : Category} (F : Cospan C) (P : Pullback_Limit F) : Pullback (unop (fmap[F] ZeroNeg)) (unop (fmap[F] ZeroPos)) := {| Pull := P; pullback_fst := (vertex_map _); pullback_snd := (vertex_map _) |}   — with the converse `Pullback_from_Universal` at line 113.  Instantiated at C^op (and `HasPushouts C` IS `HasPullbacks (C^op)` definitionally, Structure/Pushout.v:158-172) this is exactly "a pushout is the colimit of the span diagram".

evidence.intree_statement: Definition coequalizer_is_coequalizer (L : Coequalizer (APair f g)) : IsCoequalizer f g (colimit_apex L) (colimit_inj (colimit_is_acolimit L) ParY) := {| cofork := colimit_coequalizes L ; coeq_desc := fun z h Hh => colimit_coequalizer_desc L h Hh |}   — i.e. the colimit over the walking two-vertex/two-parallel-arrow shape IS the coequalizer.

Definition is_coequalizer_colimit {q : C} {e : y ~> q} (E : IsCoequalizer f g q e) : Coequalizer (APair f g) := {| limit_cone := is_coequalizer_cocone E ; ump_limits := fun N => is_coequalizer_cocone_ump E N |}   — the converse direction, so the two presentations coincide.
Record IsCoequalizer {C : Category} {x y : C} (f g : x ~> y) (q : C) (e : y ~> q) := { cofork : e ∘ f ≈ e ∘ g; coeq_desc {z} (h : y ~> z) (Hh : h ∘ f ≈ h ∘ g) : ∃! u : q ~> z, u ∘ e ≈ h }.

statement_record.book: The coequalizer is the finite colimit over the shape with two vertices and two parallel arrows.  In Set, the coequalizer of f, g : X -> Y is Y quotiented by the equivalence relation generated by y ~ y' whenever f(x) = y and g(x) = y'.  Applied to the introductory circuit, with X the set of 'connect these two' circles and Y the set of ports, the coequalizer is the three-element set of terminals resulting from the interconnection.

Program Definition ASpan {C : Category} {S x y : C} (f : S ~> x) (g : S ~> y) : Roof ⟶ C := {| fobj := fun z => match z with RNeg => x | RZero => S | RPos => y end; fmap := ... |}   — packaging an apex and two legs as a diagram of the walking-roof shape; a cospan in C is the same data in C^op (`Definition Cospan (C : Category) := Roof^op ⟶ C`, line 34).

statement_record.book: A cospan in a category C is a pair of morphisms into a common object, A -> N <- B.  The common codomain N is the apex; the two objects A and B are the feet.

evidence.intree_statement: Definition cospan_compose {X Y Z : C} (g : CospanArrow Y Z) (f : CospanArrow X Y) : CospanArrow X Z := let P := pushout (cospan_in2 f) (cospan_in1 g) in {| cospan_apex := pushout_apex P; cospan_in1 := pushout_in1 P ∘ cospan_in1 f; cospan_in2 := pushout_in2 P ∘ cospan_in2 g |}.
Definition cospan_id (X : C) : CospanArrow X X := {| cospan_apex := X; cospan_in1 := id[X]; cospan_in2 := id[X] |}.

Lemma cospan_compose_assoc {X Y Z W : C} (h : CospanArrow Z W) (g : CospanArrow Y Z) (f : CospanArrow X Y) : cospan_equiv (cospan_compose h (cospan_compose g f)) (cospan_compose (cospan_compose h g) f)   — associativity holds only up to `cospan_equiv` (apex isomorphism), which is exactly the book's second obstruction; `cospan_id_left` (line 246) and `cospan_id_right` (line 278) are the corresponding unit laws.

Lemma cospan_compose_apex {X Y Z : C} (g : CospanArrow Y Z) (f : CospanArrow X Y) : cospan_apex (cospan_compose HP g f) = pushout_apex (pushout (cospan_in2 f) (cospan_in1 g)).  Proof. reflexivity. Qed.

statement_record.book: Given cospans A -f-> N <-g- B and B -h-> P <-k- C, if the pushout of N <-g- B -h-> P exists then the composite is A -(f;iota_N)-> N +_B P <-(k;iota_P)- C.  The identity on C is C -id-> C <-id- C.  Two obstructions to this being a category on the nose: C may lack the pushouts, and pushouts are only determined up to isomorphism.
statement_record.intree: `cospan_compose` takes the chosen pushout of `(cospan_in2 f, cospan_in1 g)` and post-composes the outer legs with the two pushout injections; `cospan_id X` is the identity-legs cospan on X; the pushouts are supplied by the explicit hypothesis `Variable HP : HasPushouts C` (line 126), and the unit/associativity laws are proved only up to `cospan_equiv`.
statement_record.strength_comparison: same, with both of the book's obstructions made explicit rather than glossed: the existence obstruction is the `HasPushouts C` parameter (a CHOICE of pushout, slightly stronger than the book's mere existence), and the up-to-iso obstruction is visible in the fact that `cospan_id_left` / `cospan_id_right` / `cospan_compose_assoc` conclude `cospan_equiv`, not equality. evidence.intree_statement: Definition cospan_equiv {X Y : C} (f g : CospanArrow X Y) : Type := { phi : cospan_apex f ≅ cospan_apex g & ((to phi ∘ cospan_in1 f ≈ cospan_in1 g) * (to phi ∘ cospan_in2 f ≈ cospan_in2 g))%type }.

#[export] Program Instance CospanArrow_Setoid {X Y : C} : Setoid (CospanArrow X Y) := {| equiv := fun f g => cospan_equiv f g |}   — with the Equivalence obligation discharged by `cospan_equiv_refl` (iso_id), `cospan_equiv_sym` (iso_sym, lines 89-100) and `cospan_equiv_trans` (iso_compose, lines 102-109).

statement_record.book: Two cospans A -> P <- B and A -> P' <- B with the same feet are equivalent when there is an isomorphism P -> P' between their apexes commuting with both legs.  This quotient is imposed because a pushout is determined only up to isomorphism.
statement_record.intree: `cospan_equiv f g` is a sigma of an apex isomorphism `phi : cospan_apex f ≅ cospan_apex g` together with `to phi ∘ cospan_in1 f ≈ cospan_in1 g` and `to phi ∘ cospan_in2 f ≈ cospan_in2 g`; it is registered as the hom-setoid `≈` of `CospanCat`.
statement_record.strength_comparison: same.  Setoid rephrasing only: instead of quotienting by an equivalence relation, the library takes `cospan_equiv` as the hom-setoid equality, so "morphisms are equivalence classes of cospans" becomes "morphisms are cospans with ≈ := cospan_equiv", which is the library's standard faithful encoding.  Note the equivalence witness is proof-relevant (a Type-valued sigma carrying the actual isomorphism), which is at least as strong as the book's mere existence.

evidence.intree_statement: #[export] Program Instance Cospan_SymmetricMonoidal : @SymmetricMonoidal (CospanCat C HP) := {| symmetric_is_braided := Cospan_BraidedMonoidal |}   — under `Context {C : Category}` `{H_Coc : @Cocartesian C}` `{H_Ini : @Initial C}` `(HP : HasPushouts C)`; the `braid_invol` obligation is discharged by `cospan_braid_invol_C`, and the braiding is `mor_as_cospan (paws : X + Y ~> Y + X)` with both hexagons proved (`coprod_hexagon_aux`, `coprod_hexagon_aux_from`).

#[export] Program Instance Cospan_Monoidal : @Monoidal (CospanCat C HP) := {| I := (@Cospan_unit_obj C H_Ini : CospanCat C HP); tensor := Cospan_Bifunctor HP; unit_left := fun X => mor_iso_lift (@coprod_zero_l C H_Coc H_Ini X); unit_right := fun X => mor_iso_lift (@coprod_zero_r C H_Coc H_Ini X); tensor_assoc := fun X Y Z => mor_iso_lift (@coprod_assoc C H_Coc X Y Z) |}   — with `Cospan_unit_obj := initial_obj` and the tensor the C-coproduct; triangle and pentagon are discharged by `cospan_triangle_identity` / `cospan_pentagon_identity`.

Program Definition CospanCat : Category := {| obj := @obj C; hom := fun X Y => CospanArrow X Y; homset := fun X Y => @CospanArrow_Setoid C X Y; id := fun X => cospan_id X; compose := fun X Y Z g f => cospan_compose HP g f; ... id_left := fun X Y f => cospan_id_left HP f; id_right := ...; comp_assoc := fun X Y Z W f g h => cospan_compose_assoc HP f g h |}.

statement_record.book: Let C be a category with finite colimits.  There is a category Cospan_C with the same objects as C, whose morphisms A -> B are equivalence classes of cospans, composed by pushout.  Moreover Cospan_C is symmetric monoidal with unit the initial object of C and monoidal product the coproduct of C, with coherence isomorphisms built as in Exercise 6.18.  (The prose asserts without proof that all symmetric monoidal axioms hold.)
statement_record.intree: `CospanCat C HP : Category` has `obj := @obj C`, homs the `CospanArrow` records with `≈ := cospan_equiv`, identity `cospan_id`, and composition by chosen pushout; `Cospan_Monoidal` makes it monoidal with `I := initial_obj` and tensor the coproduct-of-apexes bifunctor; `Cospan_BraidedMonoidal` and `Cospan_SymmetricMonoidal` add the braiding `paws` and the involutivity axiom.
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-stronger: the book explicitly declines to verify the symmetric monoidal axioms ("a straightforward but time-consuming exercise"); in-tree every one of them is proved — the six naturality conditions (`cospan_unit_left_natural`, `cospan_unit_right_natural`, `cospan_tensor_assoc_natural`), triangle, pentagon, both braid hexagons and `braid ∘ braid ≈ id`.  Hypotheses differ in presentation only: the book asks for finite colimits, the library asks for `Cocartesian C`, `Initial C` and a CHOSEN `HasPushouts C` — by the generators-of-finite-colimits proposition (6.32) these are the same requirement, though the library's choice-of-pushout form is marginally stronger constructively.

statement_record.book: Since FinSet has finite colimits, Definition 6.45 yields the symmetric monoidal category Cospan_FinSet: objects are finite sets, morphisms are (classes of) cospans of functions A -> N <- B.  A cospan records which ports are connected, i.e. lie in the same equivalence class; composition is pushout and the monoidal product is disjoint union.

evidence.intree_statement: Class CommutativeComonoid (X : C) : Type := { ccomon_comonoid : @Comonoid C (@braided_is_monoidal C (@symmetric_is_braided C S)) X; delta_cocommutative_of_ccomon : braid ∘ (@delta _ _ _ ccomon_comonoid) ≈ (@delta _ _ _ ccomon_comonoid) }   — under `Context {C : Category}` `{S : @SymmetricMonoidal C}`.

Class Comonoid (X : C) : Type := { delta : X ~> X ⨂ X; epsilon : X ~> I; delta_coassoc : bimap delta id[X] ∘ delta ≈ from (@tensor_assoc C M X X X) ∘ bimap id[X] delta ∘ delta; delta_counit_left : bimap epsilon id[X] ∘ delta ≈ from (@unit_left C M X); delta_counit_right : bimap id[X] epsilon ∘ delta ≈ from (@unit_right C M X) }.

statement_record.book: Dually to a commutative monoid (X, mu, eta), a cocommutative comonoid (X, delta, epsilon) is an object X with delta : X -> X ⊗ X and epsilon : X -> I obeying the mirror images of associativity, unitality and commutativity — i.e. coassociativity, counitality and cocommutativity.
statement_record.intree: `Comonoid X` carries `delta`, `epsilon` and the three dual laws `delta_coassoc`, `delta_counit_left`, `delta_counit_right`; `CommutativeComonoid X` adds the cocommutativity law `braid ∘ delta ≈ delta` over a symmetric monoidal base.  The dual `Monoid` class (Theory/Algebra/Monoid.v) and `CommutativeMonoid` supply the mirror side the book recalls in (6.51).
statement_record.strength_comparison: same.  The library states the dual class directly rather than as `@Monoid (C^op)` (documented reason in the Comonoid header: a Monoidal instance on C^op would need extra machinery), which is a presentation choice; both counit laws are given separately where the book folds them into one mirrored diagram, and cocommutativity is exactly `braid ∘ delta ≈ delta`.

evidence.intree_statement: Class SpecialCommutativeFrobenius (X : C) : Type := { scfa_commutative : @CommutativeFrobenius C _ X; mu_delta_id : (@mu _ _ _ (@frob_monoid _ _ _ (@cfrob_frobenius _ _ _ scfa_commutative))) ∘ (@delta _ _ _ (@frob_comonoid _ _ _ (@cfrob_frobenius _ _ _ scfa_commutative))) ≈ id[X] }   — under `Context {C : Category}` `{S : @SymmetricMonoidal C}`; `mu_delta_id` is the book's special law.

Class Frobenius (X : C) : Type := { frob_monoid : Monoid X; frob_comonoid : Comonoid X; frob_law_left : bimap mu id[X] ∘ from (@tensor_assoc C M X X X) ∘ bimap id[X] delta ≈ delta ∘ mu; frob_law_right : bimap id[X] mu ∘ to (@tensor_assoc C M X X X) ∘ bimap delta id[X] ≈ delta ∘ mu }   — the two Frobenius laws, each equating one of the book's outer string diagrams with the middle `delta ∘ mu`.
Class CommutativeFrobenius (X : C) : Type := { cfrob_frobenius : @Frobenius C _ X; mu_commutative : mu ∘ braid ≈ mu; delta_cocommutative : braid ∘ delta ≈ delta }.

statement_record.book: A Frobenius structure on an object X of a symmetric monoidal category is a 4-tuple (mu, eta, delta, epsilon) making (X, mu, eta) a commutative monoid and (X, delta, epsilon) a cocommutative comonoid (six equations), satisfying in addition the two Frobenius laws (the three ways of drawing comultiply-then-multiply agree) and the special law (comultiplying then multiplying is the identity) — nine equations in all.  Such an X is a special commutative Frobenius monoid, or Frobenius monoid for short.
statement_record.intree: `SpecialCommutativeFrobenius X` = `CommutativeFrobenius X` (= `Frobenius X` + `mu ∘ braid ≈ mu` + `braid ∘ delta ≈ delta`) + `mu ∘ delta ≈ id[X]`, where `Frobenius X` = `Monoid X` (mu_assoc, mu_unit_left, mu_unit_right) + `Comonoid X` (delta_coassoc, delta_counit_left, delta_counit_right) + `frob_law_left` + `frob_law_right`.
statement_record.strength_comparison: same, equation for equation: 3 monoid + 3 comonoid + 2 Frobenius + 1 special = the book's nine. In-tree explicitly does NOT impose the extraspecial law `epsilon ∘ eta ≈ id` (header note), matching the book, and the associator/unitor insertions the book's string diagrams suppress are written out explicitly.
